judgements.why: Foundational background; Class 9 exams require explaining the pre-revolutionary system as context for all causes.
Core social structure; directly tested in cause questions and source-based questions about estate privileges.

judgements.concept: Social Causes (privilege, inequality, burden on Third Estate)
judgements.why: Standard cause category in Class 9 syllabus; appears in 'explain the causes' long-answer questions.

judgements.concept: Economic Causes (debt, taxation, harvest failures, fiscal crisis)
judgements.why: Standard cause category; examiners expect specific examples like taille, gabelle, and 1788-89 harvest failure.

judgements.concept: Political Causes (absolutism, weak leadership, Estates-General absence)
judgements.why: Standard cause category; Louis XVI's indecisiveness and the 175-year gap in Estates-General are textbook points.

judgements.concept: Intellectual Causes (Enlightenment ideas, philosophers: Voltaire, Rousseau, Montesquieu)
judgements.why: Explicitly in syllabus; students must name philosophers and link ideas (liberty, equality, popular sovereignty) to revolutionary demands.
Trigger event; exam questions ask why it was called, voting dispute, and Third Estate's response.
Pivotal moment; tested as 'how did the National Assembly come into being' and its early decrees.
Iconic event; short-answer questions ask for date, significance, and the oath's wording.
Symbolic start of revolution; always appears in timeline questions and 'why was Bastille stormed' explanations.
Explains August Decrees; tested in cause-consequence chains linking rural panic to feudal abolition.
Direct outcome of Great Fear; exam questions ask what feudal rights were abolished and significance.

judgements.concept: Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen
judgements.why: Key document; source-based questions quote articles, and students must explain principles and Enlightenment links.
First written constitution; tested on features (separation of powers, active/passive citizens) and why it failed.
Transitional phase; exams ask about political clubs (Girondins, Jacobins) and why war was declared.
Major turning point; explains radicalisation, fall of monarchy, and levée en masse. Standard long-answer topic.
End of constitutional monarchy; tested on role of sans-culottes, Paris Commune, and suspension of king.
Republican government phase; exams cover its three stages (Girondin, Jacobin, Thermidorian) and key actions.
Formal declaration; short-answer questions ask date, context, and immediate consequences.
Dramatic event; tested on trial, vote, European reaction, and impact on war and internal politics.
Major phase; exams demand explanation of causes (war, internal rebellion), machinery (Law of Suspects), and scale.
Executive body of Terror; students must describe its powers, members, and role in 'revolutionary government'.

judgements.concept: Robespierre's role and fall (Thermidorian Reaction, July 1794)
judgements.why: End of Terror; tested on why Robespierre fell, Law of 22 Prairial, and Thermidorian Reaction significance.
Final revolutionary government; exams cover Constitution of Year III, five Directors, corruption, and reliance on army.
Standard endpoint for Class 9; tested on coup mechanics, Napoleon's appeal, and transition to Consulate.

judgements.concept: Key Figures: Louis XVI, Marie Antoinette
judgements.why: Central personalities; exam questions ask about their roles, decisions, and contribution to revolutionary crisis.
Early revolutionary leaders; Sieyès' 'What is the Third Estate?' and Mirabeau's mediation are syllabus specifics.
Jacobin leaders; exams contrast their roles, Robespierre's 'virtue and terror', Danton's moderation, Marat's propaganda.
Culminating figure; tested on military successes, coup, and as bridge to next chapter (Napoleonic era).

judgements.concept: Key Terms: bourgeoisie, sans-culottes, guillotine, levée en masse, émigrés
judgements.why: Vocabulary for written answers; examiners expect precise usage in explanations and source analysis.

judgements.concept: Outcomes and Legacy (end of feudalism, rise of nationalism, secularism, Napoleonic Code, spread of revolutionary ideas)
judgements.why: Standard 'significance/legacy' long-answer question; students must structure answer around political, social, economic, and global impacts.
Exam questions explicitly ask 'arrange in chronological order' and 'write a timeline'; dates are easy marks.
